content:
Here is an idea for automatically generating theorems with tag: for a theorem that involves a associative and commutative operator (mul, add, sup...), tag @[to_big_operator] to translate it to the big operator version. For example

@[to_big_operator]
theorem Polynomial.degree_mul {R : Type*} [Semiring R] [NoZeroDivisors R] {p q : Polynomial R} :
(p * q).degree = p.degree + q.degree

-- The tag @[to_big_operator] generates the following lemma
-- This particular example is a bit non-trivial because... it needs `[Nontrivial R]` here
theorem Polynomial.degree_prod {R : Type*} {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) [CommSemiring R] [NoZeroDivisors R] (f : ι → Polynomial R) [Nontrivial R] :
(∏ i ∈ s, f i).degree = ∑ i ∈ s, (f i).degree

Also a bonus idea: @[to_pow] (need a better name if the entire theorem is additive)

-- Adding `@[to_pow]` to `Polynomial.degree_mul` generates the following
theorem Polynomial.degree_pow {R : Type*} [Semiring R] [NoZeroDivisors R] [Nontrivial R] (p : Polynomial R) (n : ℕ) :
(p ^ n).degree = n • p.degree

Would something like this be feasible? I find it useful because some lemmas in different corners of Mathlib is lacking the big operator version. Having a tag encourage people to add them as well when they introduce the binary operator version.
I think in many cases when the big operator version is missing it is because big operators are not even defined in the current file

Eric Wieser said:

I think in many cases when the big operator version is missing it is because big operators are not even defined in the current file

True, but I don't think it's an important objection: we'd be able to write something like attribute [to_big_operator] degree_mul in a downstream file like we already to for [to_additive]/[to_dual]/[elementwise]..
Is it possible to automate this transformation? Can you describe it? I guess the binary version is sort of the inductive step, and we somehow need to get the base case

Yeah I imagined it should use induction as the general transformation, but I realized my example is a case where this doesn't work right away due to the base case :melting_face: but hopefully this is more of an exceptional case?
I expect base case to be trivial in most cases, like something you can dispatch by simp
IME many of these also require Nonempty ι (e.g. #41327), but maybe we could hardcode these common exceptions
Oh then if the empty base case doesn't work by simp but the singleton case does, then the autogenerated lemma could take in s.Nonempty instead

Longer answer: the closest existing tool is bundling things into an AddMonoidHom and applying docs#map_sum. But that would not work for situations like this mixing additive to multiplicative notation, and we would need to redefine a whole lot of definitions.

Really what would be nice is to have some way to auto-discover properties of functions, such as turning multiplication into addition. I've been rolling ideas around in my head. fun_prop is the right tool in a lot of ways for answering questions about the properties of functions. But how do we get its output into an actionable form that other tactics can use it? (h : IsAddMonoidHom f := by fun_prop) works for term mode and term-mode like tactics such as apply. simp will have a hard time using it, especially if we end up with a ton of lemmas that have keys of the form ?f (op ?x ?y). (I don't even think simp accepts a key like this?) So maybe a simproc is the right solution? One that runs on every function application and does something clever and fast to determine if it's worthwhile to try and find a fun_prop? Which is more or how we use DFunLike.coe coercions, signalling "this function has auto-inferrable properties!"

For now though, I am okay with a metaprogram, perhaps more like elementwise than to_additive, that can apply this kind of reasoning.
